title: Culture, identity, power and global issues
summary: How texts express and contest culture, identity and power, how language itself carries ideology, and how to frame global issues for the individual oral.

keyterms.definition: The shared beliefs, practices, values and language of a group; a key concept of the course.
How individuals and groups define themselves and are defined by others; a key concept of the course.
A system of beliefs and values, often presented as natural or common sense, that texts can reinforce or challenge.
The capacity to influence or control others; texts both reflect and exercise it, e.g. through who gets to speak.
Dominance of one group's values so complete that they seem normal and go unquestioned.
A regional or social variety of a language with its own vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation.
Moving between languages or language varieties depending on audience and situation.
An issue of wide significance that is transnational and visible in everyday local contexts; the focus of the individual oral.
Relating to texts and readings that examine the legacy of colonialism, often giving voice to colonised peoples.
Rendering a text in another language; translators make choices that shape meaning, and works in translation are part of the course.

questions.prompt: A novel's narrator writes dialogue in standard English but renders a farmworker's speech in heavy dialect spelling. What might a critical reader notice?
options: The narrator is unreliable about the weather
The contrast may position the farmworker as less educated or less authoritative
Dialect has no effect on readers
questions.explanation: How speech is represented on the page can reflect and reinforce hierarchies of class, region or race.

questions.text: Moving between languages or varieties depending on who you are talking to is called ___.
questions.explanation: Code-switching in texts often signals shifting identities or audiences.

questions.statement: An ideology is most powerful when it seems like plain common sense.
questions.explanation: Ideas that feel natural go unquestioned; critical reading exposes the values hidden in 'common sense'.

questions.prompt: A memoir switches between English and Tagalog without translating the Tagalog. What is a likely effect?
options: It asserts the speaker's bilingual identity and refuses to centre the monolingual reader
It shows the writer forgot the English words
It makes the text a news report
questions.explanation: Untranslated words can assert cultural identity and remind some readers that they are outsiders.

questions.prompt: Match the concept to the example.

pairs.right: One beauty ideal dominates every billboard
A novel retells empire from the colonised side
A regional word for 'small' in dialogue
A poem rendered from Arabic into English

questions.explanation: These concepts help explain how texts relate to culture and power.

questions.prompt: Why can a translated poem be analysed in this course?
options: It cannot; only original-language texts count
Works in translation are a required part of the course, and translators' choices are part of the text
Only if the translator is famous
questions.explanation: The course requires works in translation, and discussing translation choices can be a strength.

questions.text: A system of beliefs and values that texts can reinforce or challenge is an ___.
questions.explanation: Asking which ideology a text supports reveals its underlying values.

questions.statement: A text that criticises a powerful group cannot itself exercise power.
questions.explanation: Protest texts exercise power too: they mobilise, define enemies and shape public narratives.

questions.prompt: Which question most directly examines power in a text?
options: Who gets to speak, and who is spoken about?
Is the text in the past tense?
questions.explanation: Control over speech and representation is a central marker of power in texts.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for analysing ideology in an advert.
items: Identify the values it treats as desirable
Ask whose interests those values serve
Evaluate whether the advert reinforces or challenges them
questions.explanation: Moving from description to values to interests to evaluation builds a critical argument.

questions.prompt: Which is the best-formulated global issue for an individual oral?
options: How the pressure to conform to gender norms limits personal freedom
questions.explanation: A good global issue is specific, transnational in significance and visible in both chosen texts; single-word topics are too vague.

questions.statement: A global issue must be significant on a wide scale, transnational, and its impact felt in everyday local contexts.
questions.explanation: These three qualities define a global issue in the course; it should not be a purely local matter.

questions.prompt: Match each global issue to a suitable field of inquiry.

pairs.left: Who decides what art is valuable

questions.explanation: The course suggests five fields of inquiry; the fifth is beliefs, values and education.

questions.text: How individuals and groups define themselves, and are defined by others, is their ___.
questions.explanation: Identity is one of the seven key concepts: identity, culture, creativity, communication, perspective, transformation and representation.

questions.prompt: A poem's speaker says: "At school I am Anna; at home my grandmother calls me Anh." What does this line most suggest?
options: A divided or dual identity across cultural spaces
That the poem is a recipe
questions.explanation: Two names for two spaces suggest identity negotiated between cultures.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of the seven key concepts of the course?
questions.explanation: The seven concepts are identity, culture, creativity, communication, perspective, transformation and representation.

questions.statement: Postcolonial readings can be applied to texts written before decolonisation, for example to expose imperial assumptions.
questions.explanation: A postcolonial lens is a way of reading; it can reveal colonial ideology in older texts.

questions.text: In the individual oral, both texts are explored through the lens of a shared ___ issue.
questions.explanation: The global issue unites the literary extract and the non-literary extract.

questions.prompt: A tourism advert presents an island's people only as smiling hosts in traditional dress. Which lens most usefully critiques this?
questions.explanation: A postcolonial lens questions exoticised representations that serve outsiders' fantasies.

questions.prompt: Why does culture matter when analysing humour in a text?
options: Jokes often rely on shared cultural knowledge that some readers may lack
Humour is never used in non-literary texts
questions.explanation: Humour, idiom and allusion depend on shared culture, so audiences may respond differently.
